items.title: Repository plugin defaults and enterprise plugin controls generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Repository plugin defaults and enterprise-managed plugin controls are now generally available in VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Trusted repositories can install and enable default plugins for contributors. Enterprises can require plugins, block plugins, and restrict installation to approved marketplaces. As a repository maintainer, you can define a plugin marketplace and default plugins so contributors don’t have to repeat setup for each project. Contributors can turn off repository defaults where policy permits. As an enterprise administrator, you can supply approved marketplaces and require or block plugins through managed settings. Required plugins are automatically installed and enabled, and users can’t disable them. Managed settings take precedence over repository and personal choices. Repository defaults are available to individual Copilot users and users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise. Managed controls are available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud for users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise licenses issued by the enterprise or one of its organizations. Learn more about plugins for GitHub Copilot. The post Repository plugin defaults and enterprise plugin controls generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot repository plugin defaults and enterprise plugin controls GA; relevant for client teams on Copilot and for agent plugin supply-chain governance patterns.

items.title: Webhook IP ranges added to the Meta API
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: We’re adding IP ranges for GitHub webhook deliveries on github.com. The Meta API now includes these additional ranges in the hooks field. If you maintain a static network allowlist for incoming webhook deliveries, add these CIDR prefixes alongside your existing webhook IP ranges to avoid rejecting deliveries: 9.234.98.160/28 9.234.98.176/28 9.234.106.48/28 If you already keep your allowlist up to date using the Meta API, no changes are needed for these additions. These ranges apply to webhook deliveries on github.com across all plans, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud. You can retrieve the current webhook IP ranges using the Meta API and follow the webhook delivery best practices. The post Webhook IP ranges added to the Meta API appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub added new IP ranges for webhook deliveries. Client systems with static webhook allowlists must add these CIDRs, or deliveries from GitHub will be rejected.

items.title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.excerpt: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model, Glimpse. It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount, co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding, co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor, Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release, frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.31%, and Claude-Fable-5.1 ca
items.why_it_matters: New visual reasoning model and benchmark from a seed-stage startup; interesting for AI product work but not a frontier API we build on today.

items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.excerpt: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [...] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders, explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai, gpt, openai, ai, llms, ted-sanders
items.why_it_matters: Commentary on model sizing and naming tiers; mildly useful context for choosing model sizes in LLM features but no concrete release or engineering change.

items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.excerpt: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase — with Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: Why do AI agents keep choosing Supabase—and what changes when the agent becomes the user? Supabase co-founders Paul Copplestone (CEO) and Ant Wilson (CTO) join swyx for their first podcast together after a $0 to $10B speedrun as the preeminent open source, fully remote Postgres platform company. We have watched them grow from a humble Firebase alternative launched during Covid, to now being a full preferred backend for AI-built applications: long-running compute beside the database, declarative schemas, Postgres storage and reliability, Turso, developer memes, community-led distribution, and product-led sales. The episode opens with swyx’s commentary on Supabase Select and the company’s journey from zero to a $10B valuation in six years as an open-source, fully remote company. swyx also discusses his seed investment in Supabase and its sponsorship of Latent Space.
